newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coal miners form 100-km chain for subsidies.
newsitem.headline: German coal miners form 100-km chain for subsidies.

text.p: About 100,000 miners and supporters formed a 100-km (60-mile) human chain across Germany's industrial Ruhr heartland on Friday in protest against government plans to reduce coal subsidies.

The chain linking the western cities of Dortmund, Duisburg and Essen was called by miners' union IG Bergbau after Finance Minister Theo Waigel, under pressure to trim the budget to qualify for European monetary union (EMU), proposed the cuts.

Miners' leaders rejected government proposals to reduce annual coal subsidies sharply from the current total 10 billion marks ($5.9 billion). IG Berbau leader Hans Berger said the industry needed at least 6.5 billion marks in annual support to stay afloat.
Some members of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) want to cut the subsidies to 3.5 billion marks and eventually phase them out entirely.
"This is not enough to prevent disruption (in the industry) and not enough to achieve a socially acceptable transition," Berger told German radio.
Berger said he hoped union leaders could meet government officials this month to reach a solution.

The FDP, which sees the subsidies as not in keeping with its market-based economic policies, warned the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and environmentalist Greens who joined the protest not to give the miners false hopes.
"It is in the interests of the workers to be honest and not to make promises that cannot be fulfilled," FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle said in a statement.
Each job in the industry costs the state 130,000 marks a year, Westerwelle said, underscoring the controversy over coal subsidies that has brought Kohl's coalition close to collapse in the past.

"These people must be given a chance to build their future once there is no more coal industry. Politicians should not limit their support to solidarity, but tackle the social and regional requirements for structural change," he said.
Current law commits Bonn to pay about 7.0 billion marks and state governments to pay 3.0 billion marks more in coal subsidies annually up to the year 2000.

Any move that would cut jobs is politically sensitive, given Germany's record unemployment levels. And the SPD, which governs the main coal-mining states of Saarland and North Rhine-Westphalia, looks set to keep the coal fires burning ahead of the 1998 elections.
Domestic hard coal, which must be mined from deep beneath the earth, costs several times as much as imports, but Bonn has deemed it right to maintain at least a token domestic industry.
The industry employs about 100,000 coal miners, down from about 600,000 in its 1950s heyday. ($ = 1.684 German Marks)
